finding.claim: The icon URL is stored with no validation and later fetched by the nightly job. An attacker can make the server send GET requests to arbitrary hosts, including internal services and cloud metadata endpoints such as http://169.254.169.254/. The response body is read into a byte array.
finding.source: The `icon` parameter of Profile.update (PUT /profile), supplied by the caller (line 11).
finding.sink: HttpClient.send with a GET to URI.create(iconUrl) in Profile.sync (lines 23-24).

trace.note: update(webhook, icon) receives the attacker-controlled icon from PUT /profile.
this.iconUrl = icon stores the value with no scheme, host or IP check.
The nightly sync() calls URI.create(iconUrl) and sends a GET to it.
The body is read with BodyHandlers.ofByteArray(), so the response content is retained.

finding.guards_checked: The only validation in update() is the regex on `webhook` (line 12). It is anchored with String.matches, and it limits the webhook to https://hooks.example.com/ plus 20 alphanumerics, so the webhook sink at line 21 is not exploitable. `icon` has no validation at all: no scheme or host allowlist and no private-IP blocking. This is a mostly blind SSRF, because the response is not visibly returned to the attacker in this file. The bytes are held in memory and may be exposed elsewhere, which I could not check because this is the only file in the repository.

verdict.reason: src/Profile.java:16 stores the caller-supplied `icon` unvalidated and src/Profile.java:23-24 sends a GET to URI.create(iconUrl). The only check (line 12) covers `webhook`, not `icon`, and the authentication on PUT /profile cannot be assessed because this is the only file. The SSRF is blind in this file.
